title: The Nihang dals
hook: blue-clad orders keeping the martial traditions and their own customs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sevapanthis: service at the center, bread earned by their own hands. Your line was service first. Did the small job get done without a word? Day one thousand three hundred eight.

Boom. Boom. Boom. You hear it before you see anything: a big kettle drum, struck slow and heavy, carried on horseback or on a cart at the head of a line. Behind it, a tall triangular flag on a pole. Behind the flag, riders and walkers in deep blue, steel at their belts and in their turbans. The crowd on the roadside steps back to let them through. Year one met the Nihangs at Hola Mohalla. Year three met the elders' army they trace themselves to. Today is the procession itself, and what it's announcing.
screen: `A KETTLE DRUM, SLOW AND HEAVY.` → `A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.`

segments.voice: Start with the word dal. A dal is an army, a host, a band that moves together. The Nihang dals are the orders of Nihangs, each with its own leader, its own camps and its own customs, and each keeping the martial life of the old Khalsa riders. There is more than one, and they don't all do everything the same way. Now the drum. It's called the nagara, and in a Nihang procession it goes in front. Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum, and that beating it was a way of saying: this is a sovereign people, and it is here. When a Nihang dal moves today, the nagara still goes first. There's a line in the Guru Granth Sahib that gives the drum a meaning. It's a salok of Bhagat Kabir. In paraphrase: the drum beats in the sky of the mind, and the aim is struck. The true hero is the one who fights for deen, who may be cut apart piece by piece and still never leaves the field. Deen is a word some readers render as the faith, and some as the helpless. Read it slowly. The drum is inside first. The battle is first a battle of the mind. And the hero stays, whatever it costs. That's what the blue army says it keeps: the outward life of the old riders, horses, weapons, the drum, and the inward reason for it. Last, the honest part. Some Nihang customs differ from the code you read in the last block. Sikhs hold a range of views about that, and some honor the dals as living memory of the Khalsa's hardest years. This path describes what they keep, and leaves the rest to the panth.
screen: `DAL: AN ARMY, A HOST.` · `THE NAGARA GOES FIRST.` · `KABIR: THE DRUM BEATS IN THE MIND.` · `A HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BLUE ARMY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a Nihang procession. That part comes after the bell, when you can find a recording. For now, settle, and breathe. Let your breath fall into a slow beat, like the nagara: in, two, three; out, two, three. With each out-breath, picture the drum sounding first inside, in the sky of the mind. Then bring to mind one person who can't easily stand up for themselves. Just hold them there, steady, while the drum keeps time. The bell holds the time.
The Nihang dals. Blue-clad orders, each with its own leaders, camps and customs, keeping the old martial life, with the nagara drum in front. Today's word.

Your line: the blue army. Today, find one recording of a Nihang procession and watch who goes first. Then, once today, stand up for someone who can't easily stand up for themselves. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

howItsDone: Nihang dals process with the nagara drum and the Nishan Sahib flag in front, notably at festivals such as Hola Mohalla, and keep horses, weapons training and their own customs in their camps.

original.note: Punjabi: an army, a host, a band that moves together.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Nihangs are a costume for festivals.
what it means: living orders, called dals, keeping the martial life of the old Khalsa riders, with the nagara in front.
what a scholar hears: Kabir's salok puts the drum in the sky of the mind first; the battle is inward before it is outward.
recall: the one who leads the band

sources.ref: Ang 1105 (Raag Maru, salok of Bhagat Kabir)

notes: Kabir's salok 'gagan damaamaa baajio pario neesaanai ghaau... sooraa so pahichaaneeai ju larai deen ke het, purajaa purajaa kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet' paraphrased. 'deen' is rendered 'the helpless'; some render it 'faith' or 'religion'. Please confirm Ang 1105 and whether to mention both readings.
'Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum' (the Ranjit Nagara of Guru Gobind Singh) is hedged; please confirm.
Year one (day 280) and year three (days 877–879) covered Nihang dress, Hola Mohalla, the Budha and Taruna Dals and camp life; today focuses on the word dal, the nagara and Kabir's salok.
'Some Nihang customs differ from the code' is stated without naming customs; please confirm the framing is fair.

Editor (y4 pass): the salok's 'deen' is no longer rendered only as 'the helpless'; the teach now gives both readings (the faith / the helpless), and the screen, match pair, myth item and fork were moved onto what the text says plainly (the drum in the sky of the mind; never leaving the field). Garbled run-on in the closing 'honest part' split into two sentences.
